notes: **Fact.** Mathematical probability of an event E is P(E) = n(E)/n(S), where n(E) is the number of favourable outcomes and n(S) is the number of equally likely outcomes in the sample space.

**Fact.** Empirical probability uses observed frequency: P(E) is approximately the number of times E occurred divided by the number of trials. It approaches the mathematical value only as the number of trials grows.
**Fact.** Addition law: P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B). When A and B are mutually exclusive, P(A∩B) = 0, so P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B).
**Fact.** Multiplication law: P(A∩B) = P(A) P(B|A). If A and B are independent, P(B|A) = P(B), so P(A∩B) = P(A) P(B). Independence is not the same as being mutually exclusive.
**Fact.** The complement satisfies P(A') = 1 − P(A). For a discrete experiment the probabilities of all outcomes add to 1.
